title: Random-forest analysis of continuous seismic waveforms identifies five previously unreported slow-slip events in western Shikoku
summary: A random-forest regression model trained on seismic waveform features predicted GNSS-derived displacement-rate changes over roughly six years in western Shikoku, Japan. Comparing detections with earlier catalogs, the authors report five previously unreported short-term slow-slip events among 23 detected episodes; GNSS deformation patterns and fitted fault models support interpreting the transients as slow slip. The paper-level result is a retrospective detection method and event set, not prospective earthquake prediction.
organization: University of Tokyo; Tohoku University; National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience, Japan

evidence.tested: A random-forest regression model trained on seismic waveform features predicted GNSS-derived displacement-rate changes over roughly six years in western Shikoku, Japan.
evidence.unknown: The study is retrospective and geographically limited to western Shikoku. Model-predicted rates can differ from observations; smoothing can make events appear longer, a practical threshold affects counts (raising it leaves two newly identified events), and the authors state that events without associated tremor may be missed. It does not establish a prospective earthquake-warning capability or a causal trigger for the event that followed the 2016 Kumamoto earthquake.
evidence.ai_role: Mapped statistical features from continuous seismic waveforms to GNSS-derived displacement rates and flagged sharp predicted increases as possible short-term slow-slip events; authors then fitted fault models and compared deformation with existing event catalogs.
